uncited: They are distinguished from their siblings by their specific approach to handling topological discontinuities: [Marching Cubes with Octree](1259-marching-cubes-with-octree.md) relies on uniform node sizing to prevent cracks, [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md) uses dynamic lookup for scattered points, [Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration](5223-hierarchical-marching-cubes-enumeration.md) explicitly separates traversal logic for faces, edges, and vertices to ensure coherence, and [2D Stitching](10249-2d-stitching.md) generates stitch cells to bridge AMR level gaps without subdividing quadrilaterals.
Builds on the shared principles of [Grid Traversal and Data Structures](10325-grid-traversal-and-data-structures.md).
Early isosurface extraction methods like Marching Cubes [30-isosurface-extraction.md] assumed a uniform grid, leading to prohibitive memory usage for sparse fields.

The integration of octrees with Marching Cubes [Marching Cubes with Octree](1259-marching-cubes-with-octree.md) allowed for hierarchical refinement, but required careful handling of level discontinuities to maintain mesh coherence.

Subsequent developments, such as [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md) and [Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration](5223-hierarchical-marching-cubes-enumeration.md), further optimized traversal for non-uniform data distributions.

In the context of Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), methods like [2D Stitching](10249-2d-stitching.md) were developed to bridge resolution gaps without introducing topological artifacts, preserving the integrity of the isosurface across varying grid densities.
